en: The *Nandika-sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmakṣema of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, at a tree named Nyagrodha.

At that time, a large assembly of bhikṣus were gathered at the Kālī Lecture Hall, sitting together among the trees to make robes for the Buddha. They thought, "The Buddha’s summer retreat will soon end; once the summer is over, the Buddha himself will say:
'The three months have concluded and the robes are finished; I shall now go to a place where there are many people.'"
Then Nandika the Śākyan heard that many bhikṣus were gathered in the Kareri Lecture Hall, sitting together among the trees to make robes for the Buddha.
He thought, "The Buddha’s summer retreat will soon end; once the summer is over, the Buddha himself has said:
'When the three months have concluded and the robes are finished, I shall go to a place where there are many people.'"
Having heard this, Nandiya the Śākyan went to where the Buddha was staying. Upon arrival, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
Once seated, Nandiya the Śākyan addressed the Buddha, saying: “Thus have I heard:

A great assembly of bhikṣus is gathered and sitting together among the trees in the Kālī Lecture Hall, making robes for the Buddha. Now, before long, the summer retreat will have ended; when the summer is over, the Buddha himself will say:”
"When the three months have ended and the robes are finished, I shall go to a place where many people gather.

Upon hearing this, I was immediately filled with sorrow and anxiety; I could no longer perceive the taste of what I ate, I lost all sense of direction, I no longer recalled the sublime Dharma I had heard, and I no longer took interest in the worldly affairs I used to attend to.
"Why is this? Because it has been a very long time since we last saw the Buddha and the bhikṣus of pure conduct.
After Nandika the Śākyan had finished speaking, the Buddha replied to Nandika:
“Nandika! Whether you see my body or do not see my body, whether you see a bhikṣu of pure conduct or do not see a bhikṣu of pure conduct, you should always practice the five internal dharmas.”
What are the five?
First, one’s mind should always maintain faith and abandon the mind of lack of faith.
Second, one should always practice pure conduct and abandon impure conduct.
Third, one should always delight in giving and abandon stinginess and greed.
Fourth, one should always possess wisdom and abandon delusion.
Fifth, one should always cultivate extensive learning and take no pleasure in not hearing the Dharma.
Nandiya! These are the five internal matters.
Having completed these, there should further be the six recollections.

What are the six? First, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, mindfulness of the Dharma; third, mindfulness of the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; fourth, mindfulness of the precepts; fifth, mindfulness of generosity; and sixth, mindfulness of the devas.
"Nanda! If a wise disciple recollects the virtues of the Buddha, the Buddha possesses these qualities:

he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the one perfected in conduct, the one who has attained bliss, the one of immeasurable qualities, the unsurpassed one, the teacher of men, the charioteer of the Dharma, the teacher of gods and humans, and the awakened one."

Whether gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, having personally realized through their own wisdom that rebirth in this body has been exhausted, they have already established themselves in pure conduct; they should recognize for themselves what must be done: that while this body remains, no further existence shall be received thereafter.
Nanda! At that time, the mind of the wise disciple is not attached to sensual desire, not attached to ill will, and not attached to delusion; thus his mind becomes upright.
When the mind of the wise disciple is upright, having attained uprightness of mind, he attains the meaning, attains the Dharma, sees the Dharma, and experiences great joy and gladness.
Having experienced joy, one gives rise to pleasure; from pleasure, the body attains tranquility;
with the body tranquil, one attains composure;

having attained composure, one attains concentration; from concentration, one knows and sees things as they truly are: "This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the origin, this is the cessation, and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
Nandi! If a wise disciple maintains upright mindfulness amidst what is crooked, abandons any sense of resentment that arises, and does not accept anything to which the mind becomes attached—
this is for the wise disciple to delight in the path and to constantly recollect the virtues of the Buddha.

"Nanda! If a wise disciple recollects the qualities of the Dharma as taught by the Buddha, it is for great peace and security; it is visible, timeless, and can be transmitted; it can be mastered by one who possesses wisdom, from which one may emerge and find satisfaction; and by relying on this Dharma, one attains liberation from the realm of conditioned existence."
Nandi! At that time, when the mind of the wise disciple is not attached to sensual desire, not attached to ill will, and not attached to delusion, it becomes upright mindfulness.
When the mind of the wise disciple is upright, having attained an upright mind, he then attains the meaning, attains the Dharma, sees the Dharma, and experiences great joy.
Having experienced joy, one gives rise to pleasure; from pleasure, the body becomes tranquil;
with the body tranquil, one attains peace of mind; from peace of mind, one attains concentration.

From concentration, one knows and sees things as they truly are: this is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Truth of the Origin, this is the Truth of Cessation, and this is the Truth of the Path leading to the cessation of suffering.
"Nanda! If a wise disciple maintains upright mindfulness amidst what is crooked, abandons any sense of resentment that arises, and does not accept anything to which the mind becomes attached—
this is for the wise disciple to delight in the path and to constantly contemplate the virtues of the Dharma."

"Nanda! If a wise disciple recollects the virtues of the community of bhikṣus—thinking that the disciples of the Buddha possess purity, possess concentration, possess liberation, possess the vision and wisdom of liberation, possess practice, and possess attainment; and that they are a field of merit for the world, such that even a small gift yields immeasurable merit."

If among the assembly there are stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), it is because one has faith that there are stream-enterers; if among the assembly there are once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), it is because one has faith that there are once-returners; if among the assembly there are non-returners (*anāgāmin*), it is because one has faith that there are non-returners; if among the assembly there are arhats (*arhat*), it is because one has faith that there are arhats. These are the men—the four pairs of noble ones and the eight classes of persons, the foremost among humanity, the stalwarts among men, teachers of men, leaders of men, those worthy of reverence, and the supreme persons within the three realms!
Nanda! At that time, the mind of the wise disciple is not attached to sensual desire, not attached to ill will, and not attached to delusion; thus his mind becomes upright.
When the mind of the wise disciple has become upright, having attained an upright mind, he then attains the meaning, attains the Dharma, sees the Dharma, and experiences great joy and happiness.
Having experienced joy, one gives rise to pleasure; from pleasure, the body becomes tranquil;
with the body tranquil, one attains a peaceful mind; from that peace, one attains concentration;

from concentration, one comes to know and see things as they truly are: "This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the origin, this is the cessation, and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

"Nanda! If a wise disciple maintains upright mindfulness amidst what is crooked, abandons any sense of resentment as it arises, and does not accept anything to which the mind becomes attached, this is for the wise disciple to delight in the path and to constantly recollect the virtues of the community of monks."

Nandi! If a wise disciple reflects upon the virtue of his precepts—precepts bestowed by the Buddha that must not be transgressed, must not be treated lightly, must not be violated, must not be toyed with, and must not be tested—the wise one attains concentration through these precepts; from concentration, he becomes detached from craving, and his mind no longer clings to the world, just as a shattered stone can never be joined together again.

"Nanda! At that time, the disciple of wisdom whose mind is unattached to sensual desire, unattached to ill will, and unattached to delusion, possesses a straight mind. When the disciple of wisdom’s mind is straight, by means of this straight mind, he attains the meaning, attains the Dharma, sees the Dharma, and experiences great joy.
From joy, rapture arises; from rapture, the body becomes tranquil."
When the body has ceased, one attains peace of mind;

from peace, one attains concentration; from concentration, one knows and sees things as they truly are: this is the noble truth of suffering, this is the origin, this is the cessation, and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Nandi! If a wise disciple maintains upright mindfulness amidst what is crooked, abandons any sense of resentment as soon as it arises, and does not accept anything to which the mind becomes attached, this is for the wise disciple to delight in the path and to constantly maintain mindfulness of the virtue of the precepts.

Nandi! If a wise disciple reflects upon the virtue of giving, thinking, "How joyful it is that I have attained birth as a human; amidst stinginess and greed, I am able to extricate myself; I harbor no thoughts of envy; I always delight in giving and what is given out of faith, I shall surely later obtain the immeasurable fruit from even a small gift, and through this giving, I shall attain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)."
Nanda! At that time, the mind of the wise disciple is not attached to sensual desire, not attached to ill will, and not attached to delusion; thus, his mind becomes upright.
When the mind of the wise disciple is upright, having attained an upright mind, he then attains the meaning, attains the Dharma, perceives the Dharma, and experiences great joy and gladness.
Having rejoiced, joy arises; from joy, the body becomes tranquil; when the body is tranquil, one attains mental serenity; from serenity, one attains concentration;

from concentration, one knows and sees things as they truly are. This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the origin, this is the cessation, and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Nandi! If a wise disciple maintains upright mindfulness amidst what is crooked, abandons any sense of resentment, and does not accept anything to which the mind becomes attached, this is for the wise disciple to delight in the path and to constantly maintain mindfulness of the virtue of giving.

"Nanda! If a wise disciple recollects the virtues of the various devas, first is the Cāturmahārājika heaven; second, the Trāyastriṃśa; third, the Yāma; fourth, the Tuṣita; fifth, the Nirmāṇarati; and sixth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin."

Whether through faith, or through purity, or through learning, or through generosity, or through wisdom—each of these practices leads to rebirth in the aforementioned six heavens. I too am able to practice these five dharmas: faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom; by means of these causes and conditions, one attains birth in the heavens.
Nanda! At that time, the mind of the wise disciple is not attached to greed, not attached to hatred, and not attached to delusion; thus, his mind becomes upright.
When the mind of the wise disciple is upright, having attained uprightness of mind, he then attains the meaning, attains the Dharma, sees the Dharma, and experiences great joy.
Having already experienced joy, pleasure arises; from pleasure, the body becomes tranquil;
once the body is tranquil, one attains a peaceful mind; from that peace, one attains concentration.

From concentration, one knows and sees things as they truly are: "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Truth of the Origin, this is the Truth of Cessation, and this is the Truth of the Path leading to the cessation of suffering."

Nandi! If a wise disciple maintains upright mindfulness amidst what is crooked, abandons any sense of resentment as soon as it arises, and does not accept anything to which the mind becomes attached, this is for the wise disciple to delight in the path of practice and to constantly contemplate the virtues of the devas.
The Buddha spoke thus.

Nandika the Śākya was greatly delighted and received the teaching; he took it to heart and constantly practiced these six recollections. Rising from his seat, he placed his head at the Buddha’s feet in prostration.
The Sūtra on Nandika the Śākya Spoken by the Buddha.
